summary: Defines a RADIUS attribute that carries an IPv6 prefix to be delegated to the user. It can be used in either RADIUS or Diameter.

plainLanguage.summary: A RADIUS attribute is a field that a network access server and a RADIUS server use to pass information about a user. This RFC defines one that carries an IPv6 prefix to be delegated to the user's own network, so that a router can pass a block of addresses further down to the customer's equipment. The attribute is number 123.

subtitle: A RADIUS attribute that hands an IPv6 prefix to a customer network to pass on further.

tldr.problem: A provider that hands a customer a block of IPv6 addresses needs a way to tell the access server which block to give, and the existing Framed-IPv6-Prefix attribute was not designed for prefixes that the customer will use in its own network.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a new RADIUS attribute, type 123, that carries a prefix length and the prefix bits. It may appear in an Access-Accept packet, as a preference hint in an Access-Request, and in an Accounting-Request packet.
tldr.outcome: The attribute can be used in DHCP prefix delegation between a delegating router and a RADIUS server, and in Diameter it is used as the AVP with the same code, taken from the code space that mirrors RADIUS attributes.

facts.label: Attribute length
facts.value: At least 4 bytes and no larger than 20 bytes

facts.label: Packets that may carry it
facts.value: Access-Accept, Access-Request as a hint, and Accounting-Request

today: RFC 4818 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2007, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the definition of the RADIUS Delegated-IPv6-Prefix attribute and its Diameter equivalent.

sections.title: What the Attribute Is For
sections.content:
This document defines the Delegated-IPv6-Prefix attribute as a RADIUS attribute that carries an IPv6 prefix to be delegated to the user, for use in the user's network. For example, the prefix in a Delegated-IPv6-Prefix attribute can be delegated to another node through DHCP Prefix Delegation.

The attribute can be used in DHCP Prefix Delegation between the delegating router and a RADIUS server, as the message sequence in the RFC shows: a requesting router sends a Solicit to the delegating router, the delegating router sends a Request to the RADIUS server and receives an Accept that carries the Delegated-IPv6-Prefix, then it advertises the prefix to the requesting router, the requesting router asks for it with a Request and receives a Reply that carries the prefix, and the delegating router passes the prefix on to the RADIUS server in an Accounting-Request.

The Framed-IPv6-Prefix attribute is not designed to support delegation of IPv6 prefixes to be used in the user's network, and therefore the Framed-IPv6-Prefix and Delegated-IPv6-Prefix attributes may be included in the same RADIUS packet.
sections.plainLanguage: The attribute carries an IPv6 prefix to be delegated to the user, for use in the user's network. For example, the prefix can be delegated to another node through DHCP Prefix Delegation. The Framed-IPv6-Prefix attribute is not designed to support delegation of IPv6 prefixes to be used in the user's network, so the two attributes may appear in the same RADIUS packet.

sections.title: The Exchange It Takes Part In
sections.content:
The RFC draws the exchange that the attribute takes part in. A requesting router sends a Solicit to the delegating router. The delegating router sends a Request to the RADIUS server, and the RADIUS server returns an Accept carrying the Delegated-IPv6-Prefix. The delegating router then advertises the prefix to the requesting router with an Advertise message that carries the prefix. The requesting router sends a Request carrying the prefix to the delegating router, which answers with a Reply carrying the prefix, and the prefix is also passed to the RADIUS server in an Accounting-Request.

In other words, the attribute appears on the RADIUS side of the exchange, between the delegating router and the RADIUS server, while DHCP prefix delegation carries the same prefix on the DHCP side, between the delegating router and the requesting router.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC shows the exchange. A router that wants a prefix sends a Solicit to the delegating router. The delegating router sends a RADIUS Request to the RADIUS server and gets back an Accept that carries the Delegated-IPv6-Prefix. It then advertises the prefix to the requesting router with an Advertise message. The requesting router asks for it with a Request and gets a Reply carrying the prefix, and the delegating router passes the same prefix on to the RADIUS server in an Accounting-Request.

sections.title: The Format of the Attribute
sections.content:
The Delegated-IPv6-Prefix attribute has a four-byte header followed by the prefix. The Type is 123. The Length is the length of the entire attribute in bytes, at least 4, to hold Type, Length, Reserved and Prefix-Length for a 0-bit prefix, and no larger than 20, to hold those fields for a 128-bit prefix.

The Reserved field is always set to zero by the sender and ignored by the receiver. The Prefix-Length field is the length of the prefix being delegated, in bits: at least 0 and no larger than 128 bits, where 128 bits identifies a single IPv6 address.

The prefix field is only required to be long enough to hold the prefix bits, and can be shorter than 16 bytes. Any bits in the prefix field that are not part of the prefix MUST be zero.
sections.plainLanguage: The attribute has four fixed bytes and then the prefix itself. The Type is 123. The Length is the size of the whole attribute, at least 4 bytes and at most 20. The Reserved field is set to zero and ignored. The Prefix-Length gives the length of the prefix in bits, from 0 to 128, where 128 identifies a single IPv6 address. The prefix field only has to be long enough to hold the prefix bits, and any bits that are not part of the prefix must be zero.

sections.title: Where the Attribute May Appear
sections.content:
The Delegated-IPv6-Prefix attribute MAY appear in an Access-Accept packet, and it can appear multiple times. It MAY appear in an Access-Request packet as a hint by the network access server to the server that it would prefer these prefixes, but the server is not required to honour the hint. The attribute MAY also appear in an Accounting-Request packet. It MUST NOT appear in any other RADIUS packets.

The table of attributes in the RFC records the same thing. The attribute is marked 0+ for Request, Accept, Reject, Challenge and Accounting-Request, where 0+ means zero or more instances of the attribute may be present, and 0 for the Reject and Challenge packets, where 0 means the attribute must not be present. The table is a guide to which attributes may be found in which kinds of packets and in what quantity.
sections.plainLanguage: The attribute may appear in an Access-Accept packet, and can appear more than once there. It may also appear in an Access-Request packet as a hint from the access server saying which prefixes it would prefer, though the server is not required to honour the hint. It may appear in an Accounting-Request packet. It must not appear in any other RADIUS packet.

sections.title: Using It in Diameter
sections.content:
When used in Diameter, the attribute defined in this specification can be used as a Diameter AVP from the Code space 1-255, that is, the RADIUS attribute compatibility space. No additional Diameter Code values are therefore allocated. The data type of the attribute is an OctetString.

The attribute has no special translation requirements for Diameter to RADIUS or RADIUS to Diameter gateways: it is copied as is, except for changes relating to headers, alignment and padding. The text describing the applicability of the attribute for RADIUS Access-Request applies in Diameter to AA-Request or Diameter-EAP-Request, and the text describing the applicability for RADIUS Access-Accept applies in Diameter to AA-Answer or Diameter-EAP-Answer that indicates success. The text describing the applicability for RADIUS Accounting-Request applies to Diameter Accounting-Request as well.

The AVP flag rules for the attribute are that it MUST be present, MAY be present, MUST NOT be present and MUST be encrypted. In the table those flags are marked M, P, a blank for must not and V for must not be present, and Y for encryption.
sections.plainLanguage: In Diameter the same attribute is used as an AVP with code 123, taken from the code space 1 to 255 that mirrors RADIUS attributes, so no new Diameter code is allocated, and its value type is an octet string. There are no special translation rules for gateways between RADIUS and Diameter: the attribute is copied as is, apart from header, alignment and padding changes. The rules about which RADIUS packets may carry the attribute apply to the matching Diameter packets.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The known security vulnerabilities of the RADIUS protocol are discussed in the proxy chaining document, in the RADIUS specification and in the RADIUS extensions document. The use of IPsec for providing security when RADIUS is carried in IPv6 is discussed in the RADIUS and IPv6 document. Security considerations for the Diameter protocol are discussed in the Diameter base protocol.

The attribute itself adds nothing new to that picture: it carries a prefix, and the strength of the protection around it is the strength of the RADIUS or Diameter session that carries it.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC points at the known security weaknesses of RADIUS and says nothing new is added by this attribute. It notes that IPsec can be used to secure RADIUS when it is carried over IPv6, and that the security considerations of Diameter are described in the Diameter base specification.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: The length of the entire attribute in bytes, at least 4 and no larger than 20.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Always set to zero by the sender and ignored by the receiver.

fields.name: Prefix-Length
fields.desc: The length of the prefix being delegated, in bits, from 0 to 128.

fields.name: Prefix
fields.desc: The prefix bits. The field only has to be long enough to hold them, and any bits that are not part of the prefix must be zero.
